<!-- slide 41 -->
# pyGenomeTracks {.divider}

[Config-driven genome browser plots]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 42 -->
## Install & Import {.smaller}

[pyGenomeTracks · setup]{.eyebrow}

### One INI file describes every track — the tool draws them stacked

`pyGenomeTracks` is the workhorse behind many of the published ChIP-seq / ATAC-seq / Hi-C figures you've seen. The interface is unusual for Python: you write a small **INI configuration file** describing each track (file path, type, colour, height), then run the CLI on a region — out comes a PNG with everything stacked, sharing one x-axis.

```bash
pip install pyGenomeTracks
```

```{.python code-line-numbers="1-4|6-9"}
# the package ships a CLI; we drive it from Python via subprocess
import subprocess, os                               # CLI driver + path helpers
from pathlib import Path                            # tidy paths
import matplotlib.image as mpimg                    # to embed the PNG result back into matplotlib

# pyGenomeTracks also exposes a Python API, but it is brittle across versions —
# the subprocess route is what the maintainers themselves use in their docs:
#   pyGenomeTracks --tracks config.ini --region chr1:0-20000 --outFileName out.png
```

This is the section to come back to whenever you have **real browser-style files** (BED / BigWig / BedGraph / GTF / cool) and you want a *publication-ready* multi-track figure in one shot. For pedagogy on the underlying primitives, the day-2 `_05` matplotlib peaks build is where you go first.


<!-- slide 43 -->
## How It Works {.smaller}

[pyGenomeTracks · theory]{.eyebrow}

### INI in, PNG out — every track is a section, every kwarg is a row

The mental model is dead simple. Your INI file is a stack of `[track]` sections; each section has a `file =` pointing at a genomics file and a `type =` (bedgraph, bigwig, bed, gtf, links, …). pyGenomeTracks reads the lot, draws each track in order from top to bottom, and gives them all the same x-axis (the region you ask for).

::: {.keybox}
[Why this design]{.tl}

- **Reproducible**: the INI **is** the figure spec — share the file, get the same picture.
- **Composable**: stack two ChIP marks + an ATAC track + a gene model with five INI sections, no code changes.
- **Genome-aware**: it knows about chromosomes and base pairs, so the x-axis is always honest.
- **Publication-tuned**: defaults are paper-quality; the tool is built for figure 1 of your paper, not for a notebook.
:::

The cost is that you can't *interactively* re-style a single peak the way you would in matplotlib. If you need that, build from primitives (day-2 `_05`); if you need the final figure, reach for this.


<!-- slide 44 -->
## Step 1 · Write the Data Files {.smaller}

[pyGenomeTracks · data prep]{.eyebrow}

### Convert `load_peaks()` to bedgraph, `load_peak_genes()` to BED6

pyGenomeTracks wants on-disk files in the canonical formats. We take the bundled signal tracks (position + three marks) and write a bedgraph for H3K27ac; we take the gene annotations and write a 6-column BED. Both go to `/tmp` so the slide stays self-contained.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-13|15-22"}
from pathlib import Path                            # tidy path helper
import pandas as pd                                 # to write tab-delimited files
TMP = Path("/tmp/pgt"); TMP.mkdir(exist_ok=True)    # work dir for this section

# 1) the H3K27ac bedgraph: chrom  start  end  value
sig = load_peaks()                                  # position, H3K27ac, H3K4me3, ATAC
step = sig["position"].iloc[1] - sig["position"].iloc[0]   # uniform 20 bp bins
bg_27ac = pd.DataFrame({
    "chrom":  "chr1",                               # one synthetic chromosome
    "start":  sig["position"].astype(int),          # bin start (bp)
    "end":    (sig["position"] + step).astype(int), # bin end   (bp)
    "value":  sig["H3K27ac"]})                      # the signal column
bg_27ac.to_csv(TMP / "h3k27ac.bedgraph", sep="\t", header=False, index=False)

# 2) the gene model as BED6: chrom  start  end  name  score  strand
genes = load_peak_genes()                           # name, start, end, strand
bed_genes = pd.DataFrame({
    "chrom":  "chr1",
    "start":  genes["start"].astype(int),
    "end":    genes["end"].astype(int),
    "name":   genes["name"],
    "score":  0,
    "strand": genes["strand"]})
bed_genes.to_csv(TMP / "genes.bed", sep="\t", header=False, index=False)
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}

<!-- slide 45 -->
## Step 2 · Write a Minimal INI {.smaller}

[pyGenomeTracks · INI]{.eyebrow}

### Two tracks: one bedgraph for the H3K27ac signal, one BED for the gene model

The INI is the figure spec. Two sections is enough to make a real picture: a `bedgraph` track for the H3K27ac signal, painted GREEN; a `bed` track for the gene model, painted INK. `height = …` controls vertical real estate; `file = …` points at the data files we just wrote.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-15|17"}
# CREATE the INI as a single triple-quoted string and write it out
INI_MIN = f"""
[h3k27ac]
file = {TMP}/h3k27ac.bedgraph
title = H3K27ac
color = {GREEN}
height = 2
min_value = 0
max_value = 1.4

[genes]
file = {TMP}/genes.bed
title = genes
color = {INK}
height = 1
"""

(TMP / "tracks_min.ini").write_text(INI_MIN)        # save next to the data files
```

Every track gets a `[name]` header — the name is just a label, but it must be unique within the INI. `file`, `title`, `color` and `height` are the four kwargs you set on almost every track type.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
INI_MIN = f"""
[h3k27ac]
file = {TMP}/h3k27ac.bedgraph
title = H3K27ac
color = {GREEN}
height = 2
min_value = 0
max_value = 1.4

[genes]
file = {TMP}/genes.bed
title = genes
color = {INK}
height = 1
"""
(TMP / "tracks_min.ini").write_text(INI_MIN)        # save the INI
print(INI_MIN)                                      # echo to the slide
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 46 -->
## Step 3 · Run It {.smaller}

[pyGenomeTracks · render]{.eyebrow}

### subprocess → PNG → matplotlib imshow → the slide

The CLI takes the INI plus a region and writes a PNG. We shell-out via `subprocess.run`, read the PNG back with `matplotlib.image.imread`, and `imshow` it onto a normal matplotlib axis so the figure inherits the deck's cream canvas and IBM Plex Mono surround. (If `pyGenomeTracks` is not on PATH in this environment the executed chunk falls back to a hand-drawn matplotlib version with the same layout — the INI workflow is identical, only the renderer differs.)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-12|14-19"}
import subprocess                                   # to invoke the CLI
import matplotlib.image as mpimg                    # to read the PNG back in
PNG = TMP / "tracks_min.png"                        # output path

# CALL the CLI: --tracks INI, --region "chrom:start-end", --outFileName PNG
subprocess.run(
    ["pyGenomeTracks",
     "--tracks", str(TMP / "tracks_min.ini"),
     "--region", "chr1:0-20000",
     "--outFileName", str(PNG),
     "--width", "20", "--dpi", "150"],
    check=True)                                     # raise if it fails

# CREATE a matplotlib canvas; CALL imshow on the rendered PNG
img = mpimg.imread(PNG)                             # load the PNG bytes
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))              # CREATE
ax.imshow(img)                                      # CALL: paint the PNG
ax.set_axis_off()                                   # no double frame
plt.show()
```

The takeaway: pyGenomeTracks does **all** the layout — shared x-axis, track titles, value-axis ticks. You bring the INI, it brings the picture.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
import subprocess, shutil                           # CLI driver + which()
import matplotlib.image as mpimg                    # PNG reader
PNG = TMP / "tracks_min.png"                        # output target

def render_pgt(ini_path, png_path, region="chr1:0-20000"):
    """Run pyGenomeTracks if available, otherwise fall back to a clean mock.
    The mock recreates the multi-track look from the bundled data so the deck
    still tells the same story when the CLI isn't on PATH in this env."""
    if shutil.which("pyGenomeTracks"):              # tool installed?
        subprocess.run(
            ["pyGenomeTracks", "--tracks", str(ini_path),
             "--region", region, "--outFileName", str(png_path),
             "--width", "20", "--dpi", "150"], check=True)
        return mpimg.imread(png_path)
    return None                                     # caller draws the mock

img = render_pgt(TMP / "tracks_min.ini", PNG)       # try the real renderer

if img is not None:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))          # CREATE
    ax.imshow(img); ax.set_axis_off()               # CALL the imshow
    plt.show()
else:
    # mock fallback: same two-track layout, hand-drawn from load_peaks/genes
    sig = load_peaks(); genes = load_peak_genes()
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 4),
                             gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2, 1]}, sharex=True)
    axes[0].fill_between(sig["position"], sig["H3K27ac"], color=GREEN, alpha=0.85)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("H3K27ac"); axes[0].set_ylim(0, 1.4)
    axes[0].spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    for _, g in genes.iterrows():
        axes[1].add_patch(mpatches.FancyBboxPatch(
            (g["start"], 0.3), g["end"] - g["start"], 0.4,
            boxstyle="round,pad=0.02", linewidth=0, facecolor=INK))
        axes[1].text((g["start"] + g["end"]) / 2, 0.85, g["name"],
                     ha="center", fontsize=8, color=INK)
    axes[1].set_xlim(0, 20000); axes[1].set_ylim(0, 1)
    axes[1].set_yticks([]); axes[1].set_ylabel("genes")
    axes[1].set_xlabel("chr1 position (bp)")
    axes[1].spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 47 -->
## Step 4 · Stack a Second Mark {.smaller}

[pyGenomeTracks · multi-track]{.eyebrow}

### Add a second bedgraph for H3K4me3 — three tracks now, one figure

The whole point of the tool is that adding a track is **one INI section**. We write an H3K4me3 bedgraph the same way, drop a `[h3k4me3]` block into the INI, and re-render. Notice how the enhancer at ~8.5 kb has H3K27ac but **no** H3K4me3 — that's the canonical "active enhancer vs promoter" pattern, and the multi-track stack is the figure that tells that story.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-7|9-26"}
# write the second bedgraph (H3K4me3) alongside the first
bg_4me3 = pd.DataFrame({
    "chrom": "chr1",
    "start": sig["position"].astype(int),
    "end":   (sig["position"] + step).astype(int),
    "value": sig["H3K4me3"]})
bg_4me3.to_csv(TMP / "h3k4me3.bedgraph", sep="\t", header=False, index=False)

INI_MULTI = f"""
[h3k27ac]
file = {TMP}/h3k27ac.bedgraph
title = H3K27ac
color = {GREEN}
height = 2
min_value = 0
max_value = 1.4

[h3k4me3]
file = {TMP}/h3k4me3.bedgraph
title = H3K4me3
color = {BLUE}
height = 2
min_value = 0
max_value = 1.4

[genes]
file = {TMP}/genes.bed
title = genes
color = {INK}
height = 1
"""
(TMP / "tracks_multi.ini").write_text(INI_MULTI)    # save INI v2
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
bg_4me3 = pd.DataFrame({
    "chrom": "chr1",
    "start": sig["position"].astype(int),
    "end":   (sig["position"] + step).astype(int),
    "value": sig["H3K4me3"]})
bg_4me3.to_csv(TMP / "h3k4me3.bedgraph", sep="\t", header=False, index=False)

INI_MULTI = f"""
[h3k27ac]
file = {TMP}/h3k27ac.bedgraph
title = H3K27ac
color = {GREEN}
height = 2
min_value = 0
max_value = 1.4

[h3k4me3]
file = {TMP}/h3k4me3.bedgraph
title = H3K4me3
color = {BLUE}
height = 2
min_value = 0
max_value = 1.4

[genes]
file = {TMP}/genes.bed
title = genes
color = {INK}
height = 1
"""
(TMP / "tracks_multi.ini").write_text(INI_MULTI)

PNG2 = TMP / "tracks_multi.png"
img = render_pgt(TMP / "tracks_multi.ini", PNG2)

if img is not None:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
    ax.imshow(img); ax.set_axis_off()
    plt.show()
else:
    # mock fallback: three tracks stacked, same colour mapping as the INI
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(8, 5),
                             gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2, 2, 1]}, sharex=True)
    axes[0].fill_between(sig["position"], sig["H3K27ac"], color=GREEN, alpha=0.85)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("H3K27ac"); axes[0].set_ylim(0, 1.4)
    axes[1].fill_between(sig["position"], sig["H3K4me3"], color=BLUE, alpha=0.85)
    axes[1].set_ylabel("H3K4me3"); axes[1].set_ylim(0, 1.4)
    for ax in axes[:2]:
        ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    for _, g in genes.iterrows():
        axes[2].add_patch(mpatches.FancyBboxPatch(
            (g["start"], 0.3), g["end"] - g["start"], 0.4,
            boxstyle="round,pad=0.02", linewidth=0, facecolor=INK))
        axes[2].text((g["start"] + g["end"]) / 2, 0.85, g["name"],
                     ha="center", fontsize=8, color=INK)
    axes[2].set_xlim(0, 20000); axes[2].set_ylim(0, 1)
    axes[2].set_yticks([]); axes[2].set_ylabel("genes")
    axes[2].set_xlabel("chr1 position (bp)")
    axes[2].spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

## Step 5 · Polish — Spacer + X-Axis Section {.smaller}

[pyGenomeTracks · polish]{.eyebrow}

### `[spacer]` adds breathing room; `[x-axis]` puts the coordinate ruler at the bottom

Two more INI sections turn the working figure into a paper-ready one. `[spacer]` adds vertical white space between tracks (so adjacent bedgraphs don't visually bleed into each other). `[x-axis]` draws the coordinate ruler — pyGenomeTracks figures look unfinished without it.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-29|31"}
INI_PUB = f"""
[h3k27ac]
file = {TMP}/h3k27ac.bedgraph
title = H3K27ac
color = {GREEN}
height = 2
min_value = 0
max_value = 1.4

[spacer]
height = 0.25

[h3k4me3]
file = {TMP}/h3k4me3.bedgraph
title = H3K4me3
color = {BLUE}
height = 2
min_value = 0
max_value = 1.4

[spacer]
height = 0.25

[genes]
file = {TMP}/genes.bed
title = genes
color = {INK}
height = 1

[x-axis]
where = bottom
fontsize = 10
"""
(TMP / "tracks_pub.ini").write_text(INI_PUB)        # save the publication-ready INI
```

`[spacer]` accepts only `height`; `[x-axis]` accepts `where` (`top`/`bottom`), `fontsize`, and `title`. Together they're a paper-figure unlock: the same data, presented with the breathing room and the coordinate ruler the reader needs.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.2
INI_PUB = f"""
[h3k27ac]
file = {TMP}/h3k27ac.bedgraph
title = H3K27ac
color = {GREEN}
height = 2
min_value = 0
max_value = 1.4

[spacer]
height = 0.25

[h3k4me3]
file = {TMP}/h3k4me3.bedgraph
title = H3K4me3
color = {BLUE}
height = 2
min_value = 0
max_value = 1.4

[spacer]
height = 0.25

[genes]
file = {TMP}/genes.bed
title = genes
color = {INK}
height = 1

[x-axis]
where = bottom
fontsize = 10
"""
(TMP / "tracks_pub.ini").write_text(INI_PUB)

PNG3 = TMP / "tracks_pub.png"
img = render_pgt(TMP / "tracks_pub.ini", PNG3)

if img is not None:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.2))
    ax.imshow(img); ax.set_axis_off()
    plt.show()
else:
    # mock fallback with explicit spacers (extra gridspec rows) and an x-axis ruler
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        3, 1, figsize=(8, 5.2),
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2, 2, 1], "hspace": 0.4}, sharex=True)
    axes[0].fill_between(sig["position"], sig["H3K27ac"], color=GREEN, alpha=0.85)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("H3K27ac"); axes[0].set_ylim(0, 1.4)
    axes[1].fill_between(sig["position"], sig["H3K4me3"], color=BLUE, alpha=0.85)
    axes[1].set_ylabel("H3K4me3"); axes[1].set_ylim(0, 1.4)
    for ax in axes[:2]:
        ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
        ax.set_xticks([])
    for _, g in genes.iterrows():
        axes[2].add_patch(mpatches.FancyBboxPatch(
            (g["start"], 0.3), g["end"] - g["start"], 0.4,
            boxstyle="round,pad=0.02", linewidth=0, facecolor=INK))
        axes[2].text((g["start"] + g["end"]) / 2, 0.85, g["name"],
                     ha="center", fontsize=8, color=INK)
    axes[2].set_xlim(0, 20000); axes[2].set_ylim(0, 1)
    axes[2].set_yticks([]); axes[2].set_ylabel("genes")
    axes[2].set_xlabel("chr1 position (bp)")
    axes[2].set_xticks([0, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000])
    axes[2].spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

<!-- slide 49 -->
## pyGenomeTracks · Takeaway {.smaller}

[pyGenomeTracks · recap]{.eyebrow}

### INI in, PNG out — the production path

::: {.takeaway}
[The recipe]{.tl}
1. **Write each data file** to disk in its canonical format (bedgraph / BED / bigwig / GTF).
2. **Write an INI** with one `[track]` section per file — `file`, `title`, `color`, `height` are the four kwargs you set on almost every track.
3. **Run `pyGenomeTracks --tracks ini --region chrom:start-end --outFileName out.png`** from the shell or via `subprocess.run`.
4. **Add `[spacer]` + `[x-axis]`** sections for the publication polish.

**Compare with day-2 `_05`:** the day-2 matplotlib peaks build teaches the **primitives** — `fill_between`, `add_patch`, shared x-axis — so you understand what a genome-browser track *is*. `pyGenomeTracks` is the **production** path: drop your real BigWig + BED + GTF files into an INI and ship a paper figure in one shot.
:::
